CSA B51 and API 510: how the Canadian code and the in-service code fit together

Direct answer: CSA B51, the Boiler, pressure vessel, and pressure piping code, is the Canadian umbrella for pressure equipment. It covers design registration (the CRN), construction quality, installation, in-service practice and repairs, and each province adopts it with its own amendments. API 510 does not replace B51. It is the in-service inspection code that refiners, gas plants and chemical sites use inside that umbrella. In some provinces it is adopted by name, and in others it applies through regulator policy or the owner's own programme.

The section above is written for inspection and NDE companies working under B51. This section is for the other reader: the owner-user, mechanical-integrity engineer or inspection lead who runs pressure vessels in Canada and wants to know how B51 relates to the API 510 programme they already use. CSA B51 is copyrighted. Nothing here reproduces clause text. The clause and annex references come from public regulator documents that cite the 2024 edition. For the wording, buy the edition your jurisdiction has adopted from CSA Group.

What CSA B51 actually covers

Direct answer: B51 covers boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping and fittings across their whole life: design and registration, manufacture, installation, operation, inspection, testing, repair and alteration. It hands the detailed construction rules to ASME and other codes by reference. Its main purpose is to give every Canadian jurisdiction one common set of requirements to adopt.

Manitoba's adoption bulletin for the 2024 edition (ITS 25-002) sums up the code's purpose in two parts. It promotes safe practice across design, construction, installation, operation, inspection, testing and repair. It also supports uniform adoption of requirements across Canadian jurisdictions. That second purpose explains why B51 reads differently from an ASME or API code. B51 sets the jurisdictional frame and leaves most engineering detail to the documents it references:

  • Design registration. Pressure equipment designs, and many fittings, are registered with the provincial authority and receive a Canadian Registration Number (CRN). The CRN system belongs to B51, not to ASME. A vessel can carry an ASME certification mark and still be illegal to install in a province until its design is registered there. See CRN registration requirements.
  • Construction by reference. Vessels are built to ASME Section VIII and other referenced codes. Piping is built to the ASME B31 codes. B51 adds Canadian requirements on top, such as toughness and impact-testing rules for carbon steel. Several provinces are still phasing those rules in.
  • Quality programmes. Manufacturers, repairers and inspection organisations operate under quality programmes that the regulator accepts. The 2024 edition added annexes on quality programmes for new-construction inspection, design examination and audit.
  • In-service requirements. B51 includes in-service inspection provisions and, in the 2024 edition, a guideline annex for a pressure equipment integrity management programme. Each province then states who inspects and how often.
  • Repairs and alterations. B51 sets the framework for controlled repair and alteration, and provinces usually point to the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC, ANSI/NB-23) Part 3 for the detailed rules.

How the 2024 edition (B51:24) is organised

Direct answer: B51:24 is the twentieth edition. It is organised around the life cycle of pressure equipment, from design through operation. The former Part 2 rules for vehicle fuel cylinders moved to CSA HGV 2 and NGV 2. The former Part 3 requirements were merged into the main body of the code. The edition also added several new annexes, including Annex Q on integrity management programmes.

Several provinces published lists of the key changes in B51:24 when they adopted it. Manitoba's list is the most complete public one. The changes that matter to an in-service owner are:

  • Part 2 removed. The requirements for high-pressure on-board vehicle fuel containers now sit in CSA HGV 2 and CSA NGV 2.
  • Part 3 merged. The former Part 3 requirements, which covered compressed natural gas and hydrogen refuelling station piping and ground storage, now appear throughout the standard instead of in a separate part. Clause numbers moved as a result. If your internal procedures cite B51:19 clause numbers, check every one of them against B51:24.
  • Cyclic and creep-fatigue service. New requirements cover boilers, and in Ontario's adoption high-energy steam piping, in creep-fatigue or cyclic service. Owners must have a lifetime in-service monitoring programme and set limits so the equipment can be monitored in operation.
  • Declaration of Conformity. The old Statutory Declaration form was replaced by a Declaration of Conformity (Figure D.6), and a new CRN application form was added (Figure D.9).

Where B51 stops and API 510 starts

Direct answer: B51 decides what is legal: registration, the jurisdictional inspection cycle, who may inspect, and how repairs are authorised. API 510 decides how a vessel is inspected well: corrosion-based intervals, CML thickness monitoring, remaining-life calculations, on-stream substitution, and repair and rerating practice. Canadian owners need to satisfy both. When they conflict, the jurisdictional requirement governs.

API 510 (current edition: 11th, October 2022) was written for refining and chemical process vessels. It sets internal or on-stream inspection intervals from measured corrosion, and in plain terms the interval is the lesser of ten years or half the remaining life unless a qualifying risk-based inspection programme sets it. It also requires an API-certified inspector to evaluate the results. B51 and the provincial regulations set a separate track, the jurisdictional one, that runs alongside:

QuestionCSA B51 plus provincial regulationAPI 510NBIC (ANSI/NB-23)
Is the vessel allowed to operate?Yes, if registered (CRN), installed and holding a current provincial certificate or permitNot addressed. API 510 assumes a legal installationNot addressed
How often is it inspected?Provincial maximum cycle or an approved owner programmeCorrosion and risk-based intervals set by the owner's inspectorPart 2 gives in-service inspection guidance; frequency is left to the jurisdiction
Who signs?A provincially certified in-service inspector, regulator inspector or insurer inspector, depending on the provinceAn API 510 certified inspector employed by or working for the owner-userA National Board commissioned inspector, where the jurisdiction uses one
Repairs and alterationsAuthorised under the provincial quality programme; often prior agreement or design registration is requiredEngineering and inspector authorisation rulesPart 3 is commonly referenced for repair and alteration procedures

In practice the two tracks are run together. A well-designed inspection plan gives each vessel an API 510 due date and a jurisdictional due date and works to whichever comes first. Ontario says this outright: its Code Adoption Document states that engineering assessments do not override TSSA's minimum periodic inspection cycle. Some provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia among them, let owners with an approved integrity management system set intervals inside their programme. Where an approval exists, it is the governing document, not API 510 alone.

How provinces bring B51, API 510 and API 570 into force

Direct answer: Every province and territory adopts B51, but each does it differently and on its own schedule. British Columbia names API 510 and API 570 directly in regulation. Alberta applies them through ABSA's AB-506 policy document. Ontario's Code Adoption Document adopts B51:24 with amendments and does not list API 510 or API 570 among its references. Check the adoption instrument for every province you operate in.

  • British Columbia. Technical Safety BC adopted CSA B51 2024 Edition effective 31 December 2024, together with the 2023 NBIC, API 510 Eleventh Edition and API 570 (Edition 5). Its bulletin states that compliance with the ASME codes listed is required in BC because B51:24 references them. BC deferred enforcement of some B51:24 impact-testing clauses.
  • Alberta. ABSA's AB-506 (Edition 4, Revision 0, issued 21 October 2025) states that the API and National Board publications it references are not adopted directly under Alberta regulation. They apply because AB-506 and other ABSA policy documents reference them. AB-506 lists API 510 and API RP 572 for vessels and API 570 and API RP 574 for piping as in-service references, alongside NBIC Part 2.
  • Ontario. TSSA's Code Adoption Document Amendment BPV-25-01 Revision 1 (published 15 May 2026, effective 15 June 2026) adopts CSA B51-24 with amendments. It requires in-service inspections of regulated boilers and pressure vessels to be done by holders of an Ontario Certificate of Competency, and it sets the maximum periodic inspection intervals. Its reference list includes ASME codes, the NBIC and API 520 and 530. It does not include API 510 or API 570, so in Ontario those codes are the owner's chosen practice rather than adopted references.
  • Manitoba. Inspection and Technical Services adopted the 2024 edition from 1 January 2025, excluding several clauses on design and impact testing. It also stated that it does not automatically adopt informative annexes.
  • Saskatchewan. The Boiler and Pressure Vessel Regulations, 2017 require pressure vessels to be inspected either at intervals set by the chief inspector or at the frequency in an owner's approved quality management system. The licensing provisions accept an API 510 certificate as one route to qualifying as a pressure equipment inspector.
  • Quebec. The Régie du bâtiment du Québec lists CSA B51, the ASME codes and ANSI/NB-23 among the codes for pressure installations. API 510 is not on that list. Periodic inspection is done by persons the RBQ recognises. A draft amendment to Quebec's pressure installations regulation was published for consultation in late 2025, so check the current text.

Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba also jointly endorsed AB-512H, Harmonized Requirements for Pressure Equipment Integrity Management Systems (Edition 1, issued 14 October 2025). It requires organisations authorised for integrity assessment to have access to the NBIC, the applicable API standards such as API 510 and API 570, and the relevant ASME sections. For prairie owners, AB-512H is where B51 integrity management and API practice meet in a single document. For a province-by-province overview, see using API 510, 570 and 653 in Canada.

NDE under a B51 programme: personnel, procedures and evidence

Direct answer: B51 points NDE personnel to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712) or another standard the regulator accepts. Ontario's adoption adds ASNT SNT-TC-1A by name. Alberta's AB-506 allows SNT-TC-1A for some methods if the owner accepts it, and sets a stricter rule for ultrasonic shear-wave examination. Agree the scheme with the owner and the inspector before mobilising.

The Canadian General Standards Board was wound down on 1 April 2026. That changed the publisher of the CAN/CGSB-48.9712 standard, not the certification. Natural Resources Canada's NDT Certification Body (NDTCB) has confirmed that it continues to certify personnel to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 without interruption, and the standard is being maintained within NRCan. Contracts and procedures that say "CGSB certified" should now read "certified by NRCan's NDTCB to CAN/CGSB-48.9712". See NRCan NDT certification and CAN/CGSB-48.9712.

The examination itself is the same whichever scheme the examiner is certified under. A B51 or API 510 inspector usually asks the NDE provider for the following:

  • A written procedure for each method that addresses ASME Section V or the referenced examination standard, reviewed by a Level III in that method.
  • Personnel certification records showing the scheme, method, level and expiry date, available to the owner, the inspector and the regulator. AB-506 requires the examiner's employer to keep these records and make them available.
  • Calibration and verification records for instruments, probes and reference blocks.
  • Readings tied to the owner's equipment identifiers, CML numbers and, in Ontario, the TSSA unique identifier. Questionable readings and areas not examined should be listed separately.

The methods are the same ones used in any API 510 programme: UT thickness surveys, automated corrosion mapping, phased array and TOFD for weld and heavy-wall examination, and MT, PT and VT for surface-breaking cracks. Industrial radiography in Canada is licensed federally by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, whatever the province. See CNSC requirements.

A worked example: one vessel, two due dates

Direct answer: Take an amine regenerator reflux drum at an Ontario refinery. API 510 might allow a long interval on the corrosion rate. TSSA's cycle still calls for a periodic inspection within its maximum. The owner plans the jurisdictional inspection on time and uses on-stream NDE to support it. The API 510 inspector then decides whether that NDE also meets the internal-inspection requirement.

Here is how the example plays out, described qualitatively. The drum is registered under a CRN and carries a TSSA unique identifier and a current Certificate of Inspection. The site runs an API 510 programme in its inspection database. The drum's corrosion history is mild and steady, so the API 510 calculation gives a long internal interval. The site's insurer inspector, who holds an Ontario Certificate of Competency, does the periodic inspection on the TSSA cycle.

  • Evaluation. The API 510 inspector trends the readings, recalculates corrosion rate and remaining life, and decides whether on-stream inspection can substitute for an internal under the code's conditions. The jurisdictional inspector uses the same data and their own examination to complete the periodic inspection and issue the Record of Inspection.

One NDE data set serves both inspectors. That only works if the report is structured for both of them, with identifiers, method qualification, coverage and limitations stated plainly.

Common mistakes Canadian owners make with B51 and API 510

  • Treating an API 510 interval as the legal interval. In most provinces the jurisdictional cycle or an approved programme sets the legal limit. API 510 cannot extend it.
  • Citing the wrong edition. BC adopted API 510 Eleventh Edition by name. Other provinces work through policy. B51:24 renumbered clauses. Procedures still citing B51:19 numbers or the old Statutory Declaration form are a common audit finding.
  • Assuming ASME stamping is enough. Without a provincial CRN, an ASME-stamped vessel cannot be legally installed. Imported used vessels have their own acceptance rules in several provinces.
  • Writing "CGSB certified" into specifications after April 2026. Certification continues through NRCan's NDTCB. Update the wording so procurement does not reject qualified technicians on a technicality.
  • Running repairs under API 510 alone. Provincial repair authorisation, design registration for alterations and NBIC Part 3 procedures apply in addition to API 510.

CSA B51 and API 510: frequently asked questions

What is the CSA B51 boiler, pressure vessel and pressure piping code?

It is the Canadian national code for boilers, pressure vessels, pressure piping and fittings. It covers design registration (CRN), construction quality, installation, in-service practice and repairs, and references ASME and other codes for detailed construction rules. Each province and territory adopts it, usually with amendments.

Does CSA B51 replace API 510 in Canada?

No. B51 is the jurisdictional framework and API 510 is the in-service engineering practice used within it. BC adopts API 510 directly, Alberta applies it through AB-506, and in Ontario it is the owner's chosen practice alongside TSSA's adopted requirements.

Does CSA B51 have an in-service inspection section?

Yes. B51 contains in-service requirements, and the 2024 edition added Annex Q with guidelines for a pressure equipment integrity management programme. Provinces then set who inspects and the maximum cycle. Ontario, for example, ties in-service inspection to holders of an Ontario Certificate of Competency.

What is a CRN and how does it relate to B51?

A Canadian Registration Number is the provincial registration of a pressure equipment design or fitting under B51. A vessel without a CRN for the province it is installed in cannot legally be installed there, even if it is ASME-stamped.

Which NDE certification does CSA B51 require?

B51 points to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (ISO 9712) or another standard the regulator accepts. Ontario's adoption adds ASNT SNT-TC-1A by name. AB-506 in Alberta has method-specific rules. Since CGSB closed on 1 April 2026, NRCan's NDT Certification Body continues to certify to CAN/CGSB-48.9712.

Does Atlantis act as the B51 or API 510 inspector?

No. Atlantis performs the NDE. The owner's API 510 inspector and the provincially certified inspector stay inspector of record and sign. Ask us to scope the NDE for your next inspection.
